case_study_insert.main_stem: Dovetail Claims Technology (DCT) is a public limited company in the insurance technology (insurtech) sector, employing a workforce of 180. Founded in 2011 by Elena Vasquez, the business supplies claims-automation software to insurance brokers and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. DCT plans to invest $2,100,000 in a new generative-AI claims triage platform, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and $600,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,300,000 a year, a variable cost of $260 a unit and a selling price of $360, and currently produces 31,000 units a year. DCT faces two operational problems: quality complaints about auto-approved claims have risen and labour turnover among data-labelling staff has reached 19%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: DCT's platform processed 1.9 million claims documents last year for 320 broker clients, cutting average claim-handling time from 6 days to 2 days. Automation accuracy reached 94.5%; customer complaints fell from 41 to 19 per month, but quality disputes over auto-approved claims rose 12%. Market research of 400 brokers found 66% would pay an 8% adoption uplift for faster triage and 57% prioritise audit-ready decision logs. A training needs analysis shows 24 of 180 staff lack generative-AI skills; off-the-job courses at the insurtech institute cost $950 per employee. Net promoter score is 54. Staff complete on-the-job training on the triage platform and off-the-job training at the insurtech institute.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Dovetail Claims Technology for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, the highest in nine years. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $13.40 to $14.10 per hour from April 2026. (3) Motor insurance claims inflation is running at 11.3% year-on-year and brokers' technology budgets grew 7.6%, while general inflation is 6.3% — insurers are under acute pressure to cut processing costs.

questions.question_text: DCT plans to raise $1,500,000 of its $2,100,000 generative-AI expansion through a share issue. Explain two advantages for DCT of the share issue rather than a $1,500,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $1,500,000 share issue raises permanent capital with no repayments and no interest, so DCT avoids layering heavy debt service on top of fixed costs of $1,300,000 a year while the generative-AI claims triage platform is still being built. Broker adoption of an 8% adoption uplift will take time to prove, and equity financing lets DCT fund that ramp-up from the 66% of 400 brokers willing to pay the uplift without pressure to cut corners on model quality — the exact failure mode behind the 12% rise in quality disputes.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads risk across a broad public investor base and signals confidence to broker clients and the market, reinforcing DCT's standing with the 57% of brokers who prioritise audit-ready decision logs. A bank loan would hand a lender security over assets and impose covenants that could constrain DCT's democratic leadership's preferred development pace; the share issue preserves strategic freedom while the retained profit of $600,000 covers the balance of the investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Dovetail Claims Technology and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: DCT is launching its generative-AI claims triage platform to insurance brokers. Consider headline sponsorship of the National Insurtech Summit, a weekly webinar series demonstrating audit-ready decision logs, or outbound telephone sales by its account-management team. Which should DCT choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National Insurtech Summit sponsorship: Headline sponsorship would place DCT's brand in front of hundreds of broker decision-makers, claims heads and regulators in one room, building high-level credibility quickly. It suits a public limited company with national ambitions. However, cost is high — stand, speaking slot, hospitality and travel — for a business already investing $2,100,000, the audience includes many non-buyers, and a single event creates no ongoing pipeline, so lead quality is uneven.

Weekly webinar series demonstrating audit-ready decision logs: Webinars directly show the 57% of 400 brokers who prioritise audit-ready decision logs exactly what they need to see — how generative-AI triage keeps a complete, regulator-inspectable trail while cutting claim handling from 6 days to 2 days. Demonstrations are repeatable, measurable (registrations, replays, Q&A), cheap per lead, and let DCT surface the 66% willing to pay an 8% adoption uplift for faster triage. Drawbacks are that some brokers screen out webinars and content quality must stay high week after week.

Outbound telephone sales: A dedicated account team can book meetings quickly and personalise DCT's pitch to each broker's book of business. However, cold calling into regulated insurance firms has low conversion, can damage DCT's premium brand, consumes 180 staff-equivalent capacity, and pushes hard before trust is built — a poor fit when buyers need to see audit-ready evidence, not hear a sales script.

Recommendation: DCT should choose the weekly webinar series. It demonstrates the audit-ready logs that 57% of brokers demand, showcases the 6-to-2-day turnaround and 94.5% accuracy, generates measurable leads every week, and scales nationally. Summit sponsorship is rejected as an expensive one-off inconsistent with a software firm funding $2,100,000 of R&D, and outbound telephone sales is rejected as intrusive and low-conversion for compliance-led buyers who prefer to evaluate evidence first; webinars also arm the sales team with warm, qualified follow-ups.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of DCT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of DCT with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the Summit sponsorship and outbound telephone sales are rejected.

questions.question_text: DCT's data-labelling labour turnover has reached 19% and quality disputes over auto-approved claims rose 12%. Explain two benefits for DCT of its democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership involves data-labelling staff in reviewing the cases that trigger auto-approvals, so the team can flag ambiguous policy wording and edge cases before models repeat mistakes at scale. Frontline input directly attacks the 12% rise in quality disputes, improves the training data behind the platform's 94.5% automation accuracy and reduces rework — while reinforcing to brokers that DCT's triage is supervised, not blind automation.

Point 2: Giving labellers a genuine voice in workload, rotation and quality targets satisfies esteem needs (Maslow) and combats the disengagement driving 19% labour turnover, which is expensive for a 180-person company where experienced labelers are scarce. Higher retention protects the consistency of the dataset, lowers recruitment and retraining spend, and keeps the flat, democratic ethos credible across the hierarchical structure — ensuring Elena Vasquez's strategy is implemented by motivated staff rather than grudging compliance.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to DCT's leadership style, labelling team and quality disputes.

questions.question_text: DCT must upskill 24 claims analysts in generative-AI supervision. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the insurtech institute. Which should DCT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training analysts on live claims under senior supervision keeps 2-day turnaround flowing and grounds learning in DCT's real 320 broker workflows and 1.9 million annual claims documents. It costs nothing in fees and is fast. Drawbacks are that senior supervisors are already stretched by 19% labeller turnover, training quality varies between coaches, and no external certificate results — a gap when 57% of brokers demand audit-ready evidence of staff competence and quality disputes rose 12% this year.

Off-the-job training at the insurtech institute: The institute delivers a structured generative-AI supervision curriculum with external accreditation, producing audit-ready certificates for all 24 analysts at $950 each — $22,800 in total, trivial against the $2,100,000 platform investment and $16,800,000 revenue. Analysts step away from live claims for course days, however, and institute content is generic rather than specific to DCT's triage engine, so supervised sandbox practice afterwards remains necessary to convert theory into flawless production work.

Decision: DCT should choose off-the-job training at the insurtech institute. The 12% rise in quality disputes is a regulated-audit risk; certified, externally examined supervision is precisely the evidence brokers and auditors demand, and $22,800 is a price well worth paying against $2,100,000 of new investment. On-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because informal coaching cannot reliably reverse a dispute trend or satisfy audit-ready expectations while seniors are overstretched; DCT can complement the course with supervised shadowing for two weeks per analyst to apply the learning to live triage queues.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to DCT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of DCT.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of DCT with a well-justified decision covering cost, audit readiness and workload.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how DCT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,300,000 ÷ ($360 − $260) = $1,300,000 ÷ $100 = 13,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 13,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $360 − $260 = $100. Answer: contribution per unit is $100.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways DCT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 13,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 31,000 units to confirm a margin of safety of 18,000 units, comfortably covering the fixed-cost burden while the $2,100,000 generative-AI platform beds in across 320 broker clients.
2. Contribution per unit of $100 lets managers model the 8% adoption uplift — roughly $28.80 per unit — and test whether brokers will absorb it, or whether DCT must offset it with deeper automation to protect the $260 variable cost.
3. Fixed costs of $1,300,000 a year and the $100 contribution can frame the share-issue business case for the board, showing how many additional licence units each $100,000 of the $1,500,000 raise must sell through before the platform breaks even at its own operating level.
4. Unit-cost data ($1,300,000 ÷ 31,000 units + $260 = $301.94 a unit) benchmarks delivery cost per licence, identifies where quality disputes consume rework effort, and supports labour-productivity tracking at 172 units per employee to rebalance labelling workloads and slow the 19% turnover.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 13,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $100 | (iii) Four contextual uses: the 18,000-unit margin of safety against 31,000 units de-risks the launch; contribution per unit of $100 models the 8% adoption uplift; fixed costs of $1,300,000 frame the $1,500,000 share issue; and unit costs of $301.94 benchmark rework from quality disputes and 19% labeller turnover.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate DCT's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has DCT's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 50.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 51.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 17.0%
ROCE 2024 = 17.4%
ROCE 2025 = 18.8%

Detailed workings: Revenue grew from $14,500,000 in 2024 to $16,800,000 in 2025, a rise of 15.9%. Cost of sales rose from $7,250,000 to $8,232,000, a slower 13.6%, lifting gross profit from $7,250,000 to $8,568,000. Operating profit rose from $2,175,000 to $2,856,000, up 31.3% — nearly double the revenue growth rate — demonstrating strong operating leverage on the claims-automation platform. Capital employed grew from $12,500,000 to $15,200,000, up 21.6%, reflecting investment ahead of the generative-AI launch, and interest payable rose from $210,000 to $235,000.

Evaluation: Profitability improved on every measure. The gross improvement from 50.0% to 51.0% shows pricing discipline and delivery efficiency at scale, and customer complaints falling from 41 to 19 per month supports that. The operating improvement from 15.0% to 17.0% shows DCT converts extra revenue into profit far more efficiently as fixed costs of $1,300,000 a year are absorbed. The return on capital employed rose from 17.4% to 18.8%, respectable though not spectacular given the capital employed jump of 21.6% — the new platform must earn its keep. Residual risks: 12% more quality disputes over auto-approvals, 19% labour turnover in labelling, and the fact that brokers' budgets may not stretch to an 8% uplift without harder proof of savings.

Conclusion: DCT's financial performance has improved. Revenue grew 15.9%, operating profit grew 31.3%, and all three profitability measures advanced. The improvement is genuine but must be defended: DCT should fix the quality disputes and labelling turnover before the generative-AI launch, because audit-ready reliability is the whole basis of its pricing power and the reason brokers will pay the uplift.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue growth, cost leverage, capital employed growth and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether DCT's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for DCT of allowing fully automated claim approval without a human sign-off step.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Removing the human sign-off would push DCT's 2-day average claim handling toward hours, a decisive selling point for the 66% of 400 brokers willing to pay an 8% adoption uplift for faster triage. It would scale at near-zero marginal cost across all 1.9 million claims documents processed annually, compressing the $260 variable cost per unit and strengthening DCT's case for the $1,500,000 share issue used to build the generative-AI platform.

Disadvantage: Full automation would remove the judgement layer that catches edge cases, accelerating the 12% rise in quality disputes over auto-approved claims and exposing brokers to regulatory challenge on audit-ready decision logs — the priority of 57% of brokers. A high-profile wrongful denial could cost DCT key accounts, damage the net promoter score of 54, and trigger contractual penalties that dwarf the saving from removing human review from the loop.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to DCT's automation accuracy, research data and dispute trend.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 5.25% to 6.0%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in motor insurance claims inflation will affect DCT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): DCT is equity-financed for its expansion — a $1,500,000 share issue plus $600,000 retained profit — so the direct effect on the $2,100,000 generative-AI programme is limited; interest payable of $235,000 could drift up on legacy facilities. The main impact is indirect: brokers and insurers face pricier capital, which may slow technology adoption even as budgets grow 7.6%. A real but secondary drag.

Minimum wage increase (5.2%, from $13.40 to $14.10 per hour): With a workforce of 180 spread across data labelling, support and junior engineering, roughly 80 staff near the minimum wage cost about 80 × 2,000 hours × $13.40 = $2,144,000 a year, so the 5.2% rise adds roughly $111,500 a year — meaningful but absorbable against operating profit of $2,856,000 and partly offset by automation gains. It also raises pay expectations across the labelling team, compounding the 19% labour turnover problem.

Motor insurance claims inflation (11.3% year-on-year): This is a demand-side shock of the first order for DCT. Insurers squeezed by 11.3% claims inflation must cut processing cost per claim; brokers' technology budgets are already up 7.6% and 66% of 400 brokers would pay an 8% adoption uplift for faster triage. Every 11.3% rise widens DCT's addressable market, strengthens the ROI case for the $2,100,000 platform, accelerates replacement of paper workflows (still capturing the market) and supports premium pricing on audit-ready triage. Claims inflation also increases data complexity, though — requiring even tighter model supervision to keep quality disputes down.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in motor insurance claims inflation will have the greatest impact. It attacks the exact cost problem DCT sells against, expanding demand, uplift pricing power and retention across 320 broker clients. The wage rise is second — roughly $111,500 a year of unavoidable cost — while the interest-rate rise is the smallest for an equity-financed PLC. DCT should respond by accelerating the generative-AI launch, marketing ROI explicitly against claims inflation, and tightening human supervision to hold disputes flat while volume surges.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to DCT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on DCT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of DCT with a well-justified judgement that claims inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
